h.select_rule: Discard any hypothesis whose condition is the edited field's own current value, or whose condition merely disables or disconnects the edited component. From the rest, keep 10 with distinct mechanisms and field pairs, favouring those where an informed expert could plausibly bet on either direction.
h.strategy: Two patterns are banned because experts find them obvious: (1) conditioning on the current value of the same field being edited, which just restates that upgrading a weak setting helps more than upgrading a strong one; (2) conditions that make the edited component unused, unreachable or inert. Instead, each hypothesis must link two DIFFERENT fields that interact through a non-trivial mechanism, such as substitution between parallel routes, a capacity already supplied elsewhere, one part acting as a bottleneck for another, or interference that turns a usually helpful edit harmful. No condition setting may appear in more than two hypotheses. Use the gaps and negated assumptions as the source of each idea. In each 'why', name the mechanism and explain why the opposite direction is also a priori plausible.

hyps.why: With Adam each weight moves ~lr per step so the output change scales with fan-in, making wide nets diverge sooner when LR is raised.
Large batches give few updates per epoch and low-variance gradients, so bigger steps are both needed and safe.
Update effects compound across layers, so three-layer nets have a smaller stable LR range and suffer more from a step up.
sklearn applies L2 per minibatch, so larger batches mean fewer penalty applications per epoch, relieving over-shrinkage at high alpha.
Small batches at high LR combine large steps with high gradient variance, pushing training toward divergence.
Under a fixed 243-epoch budget a deeper net with tiny steps stays undertrained, so added depth cannot be exploited.
Narrow layers are a capacity bottleneck that an extra layer compensates for, whereas wide nets already have ample capacity.
Strong L2 shrinks every layer's weights, and stacking another shrunken layer compounds signal attenuation toward a constant predictor.
Wider layers change their outputs more per Adam step, partially offsetting the slow progress of tiny-LR training.
The L2 term sums over all weights, so widening under heavy alpha increases total shrinkage pressure and renders added units inert.
